title: 25th Hour
full_review:
"25th Hour" (Touchstone) is an engaging urban parable charting the final 24 hours of freedom of a convicted New York drug dealer, Monty Brogan (Edward Norton), struggling to redeem his life and tattered personal relations.

Directed by Spike Lee and based on the novel by David Benioff, the film explores the cause-and-effect reciprocity inherent in the decisions one makes in life, and the consequences reverberating from them. Despite the unsavory nature of the role, Norton delivers a compelling performance, infusing an otherwise unsympathetic character with humanity and genuine emotion.

Much of the story's action hinges on Monty's relationship with his two closest friends, both of whom have known him since childhood: Jacob (Philip Seymour Hoffman), a frumpy high school teacher tormented by a Lolita-like attraction to one of his students (Anna Paquin), and Slaughtery (Barry Pepper), a suave Wall Street cowboy with an inflated self-image. Also in the mix is Monty's girlfriend, Naturelle (Rosario Dawson), a sultry Puerto Rican bombshell whom he suspects tipped off the police.

The final player in Monty's crumbling house of cards is his estranged father, James Brogan (Brian Cox), a meat-and-potatoes ex-firefighter turned pub proprietor. Still entertaining high aspirations for Monty, he desperately seeks reconciliation and forgiveness for his own past indiscretions -- a drinking problem following his wife's death -- which may have contributed to his son's fall from grace.

In a final sequence, while en route to prison, Monty's father offers him one last chance at escape. Reminiscent of Martin Scorsese's "The Last Temptation of Christ," he paints an alternative ending to Monty's life story -- one more attractive, but morally bankrupt. Monty, like Christ, rejects the temptation and accepts his fate.

But Monty Brogan, though charismatic, remains an enigma throughout the film. While the back story pertaining to his arrest is told via flashbacks, very little is offered, beyond his father's bout with the bottle, in the way of an explanation as to why a student with such academic and athletic promise would choose such a ruinous path. One is also left wondering whether Monty would have atoned by his own volition or if his remorse is merely prompted by his frustration over being caught. While Norton comes across as contrite, it may prove difficult for audiences not to question his sincerity.

Disturbingly, with one brief exception, the film shies away from showing the human toll exacted by Monty's drug-related crimes. While not detracting from the narrative, this omission leaves a bad taste -- a more balanced depiction would have given the character greater depth by accentuating his moral dilemma in sharper terms -- not to mention being more intellectually honest.

Taking into account the reality of living in New York City after the Sept. 11 terror attacks, the film is replete with imagery reflecting the solemn tenor of the city. In one scene, Jacob and Slaughtery have a conversation about Monty eerily framed by a window overlooking ground zero. From their dialogue one suspects Lee is trying to draw a parallel between Monty and the country, as if both share complicity in their own tragic turn of events.

Lee once again displays a knack for creating thought-provoking drama through bold visuals. While cinematographer Rodrigo Prieto deserves credit for capturing the many textures of New York City, the score by Terence Blanchard at times borders on the melodramatic.

To emphasize the good, the film pulls no punches in making a clear-cut statement about taking responsibility for one's actions. Lee drives home this point during a pub restroom scene.

Echoing Lee's earlier "Do The Right Thing," Monty stands staring at his reflection in the mirror like a modern-day Hamlet and launches into a rabid tirade of racial, ethnic and religious slurs, implicating every possible demographic in his downfall. Then, realizing he must solely bear the blame for the choices he made, he hurls one last invective at himself. While some might find the diatribe offensive, especially his vitriolic criticism of the Catholic Church, Monty's soul-searching epiphany not only reveals his inner turmoil, but makes a powerfully blunt, albeit ineloquent, case for personal accountability.

Another important insight is offered by the character of Slaughtery. Confronting Naturelle in a nightclub, he argues that by not voicing opposition they aided and abetted Monty's demise. Seduced by the allure of the lifestyle Monty's street prestige afforded him, Slaughtery laments not only his silence, but the ruining of lives his silence facilitated. He comes to the sobering realization that, ultimately, we are our brother's keeper.

Due to sporadic violence, a character's angry anti-Catholic remarks, crude sexual references and situations, and recurring rough language and profanities, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
